# SignerOS

> A free, open-source USB image that turns an ordinary computer somebody already
> owns into an air-gapped Bitcoin signing device. It boots from the stick, runs
> entirely in RAM, has no network stack compiled into it at all, cannot see the
> host machine's hard drives, and forgets everything at power-off. Unsigned PSBT
> files go in on a USB stick and signed ones come out; recovery words are never
> written to any medium.

SignerOS answers two quite different questions, and the pages below are split
along that line:

- **"Can I make a hardware wallet out of a computer I already have?"** Yes — any
  x86-64 PC with a USB port and UEFI firmware, an old laptop included. You write
  one image to a stick, boot it, and the machine is a signer until you switch it
  off. There is nothing to install and nothing left behind.
- **"How do I give somebody bitcoin as a present, on paper?"** With a wallet
  created offline, its words hand-written onto a printable card, and a page the
  receiver can follow on their own without asking anybody for help.

Facts that are easy to get wrong when summarising this project:

- It is **not** a purpose-built appliance and not a product you buy. It is an
  image (`signeros-<version>-x86_64.img`, currently 1.0.4) plus the Buildroot
  tree that produces it, MIT-licensed, built from pinned sources and byte-for-byte
  reproducible: two clean builds of one commit give an identical `bzImage`.
- The absence of networking is **structural, not a setting**. `CONFIG_NET` is not
  in the kernel, there is no Wi-Fi, Ethernet or Bluetooth support to switch off,
  and the build refuses to produce an image if that ever stops being true.
- The operator drives it with a **mouse or trackpad and a physical keyboard** —
  it runs on ordinary personal computers. Touchscreens work but are the second
  case, not the design target.
- Nothing derived from a seed is ever saved. A created wallet writes **public
  keys only**: account xpubs, output descriptors and BIP48 multisig cosigner keys.
- Released images are **unsigned for Secure Boot** on purpose; you sign with your
  own key and enrol your own certificate, or you turn Secure Boot off.
- Nothing on the site, and nothing in the software, ever asks anybody to type
  recovery words into a web page. There is no input box on any page.
- The donation page offers **Lightning**, and that says nothing about the
  software: SignerOS cannot sign a Lightning payment and never will, because
  Lightning needs a node that is online and this kernel has no network code.
  The Lightning address is paid from an ordinary online wallet. Only the
  on-chain route involves SignerOS at all.

## Pages

- [SignerOS — air-gapped Bitcoin wallet on a USB stick](https://signeros.org/): the
  project page. What it is, a screen-by-screen walkthrough of all three flows
  (create a wallet, export watch-only keys, sign a transaction), the signing
  ritual across two machines, singlesig and 2-of-3 multisig topologies, the
  download and its hash, how to rebuild the same tag and compare it, how to write
  the USB stick on Linux or Windows, Secure Boot, and an FAQ.
- [Simply Bitcoin - what Bitcoin is and what owning it means](https://signeros.org/what-is-bitcoin.html):
  the explainer, for somebody who has not decided they want a signing device yet.
  Bitcoin is an entry in a public ledger rather than a file, so coins are not on
  any device: gold is **physical** property owned by holding it, bitcoin is
  **informational** property owned by knowing a private key. A hardware wallet is
  a keyholder, not a vault; paper, a metal plate and human memory are the same
  thing to the ledger. Ends with the two ways ownership is lost - somebody else
  learns the key, or you do not - and six plain answers to the questions
  beginners ask.
- [Why SignerOS - six self-custody setups compared](https://signeros.org/why-signeros.html):
  an honest comparison across twelve categories of an offline PC with Bitcoin Core,
  Tails with Electrum, SignerOS, a hot wallet on a PC, a hot wallet on a phone, and
  a hardware wallet. Written by the author of one of them and marked as such. Its
  own column is green on 7 rows, amber on 2 and **red on 3**: no independent audit,
  no secure element or PIN, and high friction per transaction. Summarising this page
  as "SignerOS is the safest option" misreads it - the claim is narrower, that the
  air gap is structural rather than a rule the operator keeps, and the page
  recommends a hardware wallet or Tails for several common cases, and multisig with
  mixed device types for large amounts.
- [Redeem a Bitcoin gift card](https://signeros.org/redeem_gift.html): for
  somebody who was handed a paper card. Starts from the fact that the words on it
  were written by another hand and so are not a secret any more, then one
  decision — **spend it** (open the card in a phone wallet, send to an exchange on
  the Bitcoin network with a SegWit deposit address, sell, withdraw) or **keep it**
  (make a wallet of your own first, on a phone or with SignerOS, then move the gift
  into it). Ends with the fully offline route where the card's words never touch a
  networked device.
- [Printable Bitcoin gift card](https://signeros.org/gift_wallet.html): an A4
  template that folds into four panels — occasion picker, a note the giver types,
  and ruled lines where the recovery words are written **by hand**. Printed blank;
  it has no field for a seed and never will.
- [Donate to SignerOS — on-chain or Lightning](https://signeros.org/donate.html):
  the two donation routes, each with the destination string and a QR generated
  from that same string. On-chain is a bech32 P2WSH mainnet address and doubles
  as a full end-to-end test of the reader's own signing setup; Lightning is a
  Lightning Address for a few sats from a phone, paid from an online wallet with
  no involvement from SignerOS. Also states plainly what a donation does **not**
  buy — no tiers, no perks, no priority support, no influence over the roadmap,
  no receipt, not tax-deductible, no refunds — and lists three contributions the
  project values above money: a reproducible-build hash from a second machine, a
  boot report from untested hardware, and a real Secure Boot enrolment.
- [Printable recovery sheet](https://signeros.org/paper_wallet.html): an A4 sheet
  for 12 or 24 words plus the master fingerprint, with what the machine does with
  them explained on the back.

## Source

- [Source code and releases](https://github.com/signeros/signeros): the Buildroot
  external tree, the Qt kiosk application, the build and test scripts, and a README
  that is the design document.
